notes: A stream report after each stream: how long it was, the upload rate over the stream as a graph, frames dropped, each destination's figures and how long each scene was live. The earlier ones are in Settings › Streaming › Your stream.
Record while streaming (on unless you turn it off): a recording starts with the stream and stops with it.
Chapters at scene changes: each time the live scene changes, the recording gets a chapter named after it, in the MP4 copy.
Be right back: a button under Start streaming (and a hotkey) switches to the scene you choose for it and mutes your microphones; pressed again, it goes back.
Going live at a set time: timers can count down to it for a Starting soon scene, and Capture can start streaming by itself at that time.
New timer modes for designs: Until going live, Time left in the stream (from the length you set) and Next stream (for an end screen).
Mute while this scene is live (right-click a scene): music or any sound source is left out while that scene shows, and comes back when it doesn't.
A hotkey to show or hide any source in the scene that's live.
The greyed-out Virtual camera placeholder is gone (not planned).

Undo and redo: Ctrl+Z undoes moving, resizing, hiding, adding and removing sources and scenes, and changes to their settings; Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z) redoes. Up to 50 steps, kept until you switch scene collection. Switching scenes isn't counted as a change.
Each row in the Sources panel starts with a small live picture of that source.

Test my setup (Settings): one page that checks each source in the scene, each sound source with a live meter, a test chime in your headphones (never streamed or recorded), and what recording and streaming will use.
When the video can't keep up, the line under the preview says why in plain words (the graphics card is busy, the processor is busy, too much to draw), and its tooltip says what to do about it.
A compact layout with tighter rows and buttons for laptop screens: Settings › Appearance › Compact layout (Automatic, On or Off).
Capture's window appears as soon as you open it, and shows that it's opening while your scenes, video and sound start.
What's new: after an update, Capture shows that version's changes once. About lists them too.
If Capture ever has to close, it offers to open again straight away. Your scenes are saved as you go, so they open as they were.
Pages (Settings, the Library, the designer) and panels fade in gently when they open.
Double-click a source to change it: a design opens in the overlay designer, and anything else shows its settings menu. Renaming is still F2 or the menu.
While you're live, the preview has a red outline and a LIVE tag, and a large timer under Start streaming shows how long you've been on.
Bigger Start recording and Start streaming buttons.
The + menu for sources is sorted under headings: Capture, Designs and pictures, Video and sound, Animated backgrounds, and From your other scenes.

Tooltips: rest the pointer on the main buttons to see what they do, with your hotkey if you've set one. Every audio filter setting (Threshold, Ratio, Attack and the rest) explains itself in plain words.
The Library shows each file's size, and the length of videos, music and sounds. It also opens on the folder you were last in.

Fixed: music and other sound played from files skipped and crackled, especially FLAC and WAV files. Sound was handed to the mixer in large blocks, and the mixer, keeping the delay down, cut most of each block away. It now goes in a little at a time, just ahead of when it plays. In a test with a steady tone, the dropouts went from about 19 a second to none.

Music and video files are now heard in your headphones as well as on stream: the monitor is switched on for them, including the ones you already have. You can still turn it off for any of them from its row in the audio mixer, and that choice is kept.

Fixed: in 0.10.28 the aurora sky, Aurora pulse and Aurora wave showed “The aurora couldn't be drawn … syntax error: unexpected token 'line'” instead of the aurora. A name in the new wave's graphics-card code is a reserved word for Windows' shader compiler; it's renamed, and every shader Capture makes is now checked for those words before release.

The Writing progress overlay shows the chapter's own word count, at the right of the CHAPTER line, kept up to date from Writing Studio as you write. Writing progress overlays you already have get it automatically, styled like their label. Your own designs can use {chapterwords} (3,214) or {chapterline} (3,214 words).

Aurora wave: three ribbons of aurora light flow across the screen like a sound wave, each swelling where its part of the music is loud (bass on the left, treble on the right), with a soft glow and faint rays rising from them. Add it from Sources (+ › Aurora wave), or switch any Aurora pulse between Pulse and Wave from its right-click menu.
Fixed: clicking a chat element in the overlay designer closed NorthRay Capture with “Windows error 0xC0000005”. The panel's heading had no name for the chat kind of element.

Chat bubbles: choose Left, Right or Split (your own messages on the right and viewers' on the left, like messages on a phone) under Bubbles in the chat element's settings. Each bubble is as wide as its message, with the text starting at the bubble's left. The Chat box overlay starts on Left; chat boxes made before keep following Align until you choose.

If NorthRay Capture (or another NorthRay app) ever has to close, its crash report now says where it happened, so the problem can be found and fixed. It records program locations only, never your files or data.

Capture keeps in step with Writing Studio by itself: the book, chapter and words on your overlays change within a few seconds of you switching chapter, changing book or writing, with nothing to set up.

A new overlay, Writing progress (Overlay design… › On stream): the chapter you're on, today's words against your daily goal, the words in the book so far and your writing streak. New Reading and writing scenes include it.

Overlay text can use {chapter}, {today} (“1,240 of 2,000 words today”), {goal}, {bookwords}, {bookline} and {streakline}, alongside {book}, {series}, {words} and {streak}. When Writing Studio isn't there, they're empty rather than showing the braces.

Template packs: in the Library, Export folder… (or Export all…) saves a folder of your library, with the folders inside it, as one .nrpack file to keep or share. Import a pack… adds one into Packs, keeping its names, folders and tags. Nothing in a pack can choose where its files go.
Overlay designs in the Library show the design itself.

The NorthRay library (top bar › Library): one media library for all the NorthRay apps. Add pictures, videos, music and sounds (they're copied in, so they stay put), and save overlay designs into it from the designer (To the library). Sort them into folders, tag them, and search. Click one to add it to the scene as the right kind of source.
About no longer says Capture is at Milestone 2.

The aurora pulse (Add a source › Aurora pulse): the aurora sky moving with your Stream mix. The curtains rise and brighten with the music, bass on the left and treble on the right, and the whole sky glows with the loudness. It's drawn on the graphics card in your brand colours, with the same speed, brightness, stars and colour options as the aurora sky.
The Radio show scene template now uses the aurora pulse.

The book card fills itself in from NorthRay Writing Studio: the book you're writing, its series line ("Book One of The Alvora Chronicles") and its cover. Writing Studio's today's words and streak are there too, as {words} and {streak}. Without Writing Studio, Your details' Book and Series are used.
Pictures in designs can be named by a value, such as {cover}.

Scene templates (the Scenes panel's + › From a template): Gaming, Just chatting, Art, Reading and writing, and Radio show. Each makes a whole scene: your screen or the aurora sky, your camera with a facecam frame that follows it, and the overlays that suit it (chat, now playing, your name, socials). An existing camera or screen capture is reused; with no camera, those parts are left out and you're told.
Two new overlay designs: Book card (cover, {book} and {series}) and Show title ({show} and {episode}, with an on-air badge). Your details now has Book, Series, Radio show and Episode.

The brand kit now holds videos (Brand kit… › Videos): a transition stinger with the point where the scene switches, and an intro and an outro. Transition › Stinger › Your brand kit's stinger uses the kit's, so changing the kit changes it.
Add a source › Your intro video / Your outro video: plays once from the start each time its scene goes live, and follows the kit.

Video and sound sources finally have their menu (right-click › Video or sound): pause, play, from the start, next file, loop, shuffle, choose other files, and the new Play from the start when its scene goes live. The controls were built in 0.8.3, but no menu offered them.

Items can follow another item: right-click a facecam frame › Follow another item › your camera, and moving, resizing or turning the camera takes the frame with it, in the same place around it. Moving the frame itself changes where it sits. Works in chains (a name tag following the frame) and is kept when scenes are duplicated, exported or imported.

The aurora sky (Add a source › Aurora sky): a live, animated aurora background drawn on the graphics card, for holding scenes like Starting Soon. Curtains of light drift and ripple over a night sky with a few twinkling stars, in your brand kit's colours (following it when you change the kit). Right-click it for speed, brightness, stars and colours of its own.

Global hotkeys (Settings › Hotkeys) that work even while a game has the focus: switch to a scene, start or stop streaming or recording, add a marker, mute or unmute a sound source, play or stop soundboard sounds, and studio mode's send-the-preview-live. Press the keys to assign them. Letters and numbers need Ctrl or Alt, so typing elsewhere isn't affected, and a combination another program already holds is shown in red. A Stream Deck's built-in Hotkey action can press them; a dedicated Stream Deck plugin isn't included.

Automation (Settings › Automation): rules that switch the scene when a program opens or closes, such as "When Krita opens, switch to Art" or "When the game closes, switch to Just chatting". Pick a program with a window open, Writing Studio, or type a file name. A rule can apply only while you're live or recording. Programs already open when Capture starts don't count as opening; in studio mode it changes the program scene.

An optional pre-live checklist (Settings › Streaming): Start streaming first shows what Capture checked for itself (where you're going live, missing stream keys or server addresses, an empty scene, a mic that's muted, unplugged or not in the stream's sound, a "say something" mic check that turns green when it hears you, and whether there's a hardware encoder) next to your own list to tick, which you can add to. It never stops you going live.
Settings › Recording no longer says an MP4 copy is planned (it's been there since 0.10.7).

Save a design as an animated GIF (Save as GIF in the designer): its entrances at 25 frames a second, then the finished look held for a moment, looping, at most 800 wide, in Pictures › NorthRay Capture. Parts that are see-through stay see-through. (WebM isn't included: Windows has no WebM encoder, so it would mean bundling one.)

The aurora sweep transition: a shimmering, gently waving band of aurora light crosses the picture and the new scene is behind it. It's in your brand kit's main and second colours, and goes left, right, up or down (Transition › Aurora sweep).
Green screen on any item (right-click it › Green screen): green or blue presets, or Pick the colour from the preview, which reads your actual screen's colour where you click.

It compares colour, not brightness, so shadows on the screen go too; soft edges for hair; and the green tint that bounces onto you is taken out. How much is cleared, the edge softness and the tint removal can be adjusted.
It runs on the graphics card along with borders, so the two work together.

Voice effects as filters on any sound: Reverb (a room around you, from a booth to a hall), Pitch shift (a deeper or higher voice, up to an octave either way) and Radio voice (a walkie-talkie or old radio, with crackle if you like).
Like every filter they can be switched on and off, adjusted, reordered, and mixed with the dry sound.
A soundboard: buttons that play short sounds into your stream (the Soundboard panel, from the Layout menu). Sounds overlap, pressing one again restarts it, and Stop all stops them.

It starts with 12 sounds made by NorthRay (chime, ding-dong, fanfare, level up, drum roll, ba-dum-tss, whoosh, applause, wrong answer, sparkle, heartbeat, page turn), free to use on stream. Add your own files (MP3, WAV, M4A, FLAC, OGG); right-click a button to rename, replace, move or remove it.
The soundboard is a channel in the mixer: its volume, mute, filters, auto-duck and where it's sent work like any other sound.

A setup wizard (Settings › Setup wizard…): tell it whether you stream, record or both, test your connection, and it suggests a frame rate, canvas and bitrates for this PC, with the reasons, applied in one click.

The connection test streams to Twitch's bandwidth test for 20 seconds (Twitch receives it but never shows it; your channel doesn't go live) and measures what your connection keeps up with. Or type a speed from any speed test.
It never changes the canvas of scenes you've already laid out; it tells you where to change it if you want to.

Profiles: sets of settings (frame rate, sound outputs, recording, streaming destinations, transitions) you switch between from the top of the window. Make one as a copy of another, rename or delete it. Each has its own copy of its stream keys.
Scene collections: switch between sets of scenes and sources (each with its own canvas) from the top of the window; start an empty one or a copy, rename, or delete (to the Recycle Bin).
Recordings are named after the profile and the time, e.g. “Art stream 2026-11-15 14-00-05”.

An MP4 copy of every recording: when you stop, Capture makes an MP4 beside the MKV for editors and uploading. It's copied, not re-encoded, so there's no loss and it's quick; the MKV is kept because it survives crashes. Switch it off under Settings › Recording.
Markers: while recording, Add a marker in Controls. Each one becomes a chapter in the MP4.

The MP4 plays as it downloads (its index is at the front), keeps every audio track with its name (the first plays by default), and keeps tracks that start late in step. A recording cut short by a crash converts too.

Auto-duck: any sound source can get quieter while another has sound, usually music under your microphone. Choose it in the source's mixer menu (6, 12, 18 or 24 dB); the mixer shows how far it's ducked.
It eases down in under a tenth of a second, waits 0.4 s after you stop, and comes back over 0.7 s, without clicks. A muted microphone never ducks anything.
Music (a folder of songs): every song in a folder, shuffled and looping at half volume, ducking under your microphone straight away, with now playing for your overlays.
Now playing: while music plays in a video or sound source, any design can show {song} and {artist}, read from the file's tags or from a name like “Artist - Title.mp3”.
A Now playing template (a card with a music icon, the song and the artist, in your brand colours), and a page option to show a design only while music plays.
A Chat panel: read your Twitch chat inside Capture while you stream. Turn it on from the Layout menu.
Names in each viewer's colour (kept readable in the light and dark themes), marked streamer, mod, VIP or sub; deleted messages, timeouts and bans disappear here too.
Read-only, without signing in. Reply on Twitch… opens Twitch's own chat window in your browser. Saved layouts keep their panel widths.
Live Twitch chat in overlay designs: add a Chat element (or the Chat box template) and it shows your channel's chat as it happens, on cards in your brand colours with each viewer's name colour.
Read-only and without signing in: Capture reads chat the way Twitch lets anyone watch it, and never posts. Deleted messages, timeouts and bans disappear from the overlay too.
Choose how many messages show, whether they fade after a while, the cards' colour and the name colours. Emotes show as their names for now.
A brand kit for your overlays: six colours, a heading and a body font, font files from your library (used without installing them) and your logo, under Brand kit… in the designer.
Every template follows the brand kit, so changing your main colour or heading font restyles them all at once; a new Logo watermark template shows your logo.
Brand colours come first in every colour menu, with brand gradients; any design can follow the kit or stop following it (keeping how it looks).

Timers in overlay designs: a countdown for a length or to a time (like 20:00), a stopwatch, time live, or a clock with the date. Countdowns pulse for the last ten seconds, show your words at zero, and can switch to another scene.
QR codes from any link (or {website} from your details), drawn crisp so phones can read them.
Twenty built-in icons (star, heart, arrow, chat, music, camera, book, brush and more) that take any colour or gradient.

Overlay designer: Sources › + › Overlay design… Start from a template (Starting Soon, Be Right Back, Ending, a lower third, a facecam frame, a socials bar, a Twitch panel or an offline banner) or an empty page.

Design with text, rectangles, ellipses and pictures: colours or gradients (straight or round, with see-through colours), outlines, rounded corners, soft shadows, rotation and opacity. Drag to move with snapping guides, resize from the corner, and arrange layers. Ctrl+Z undoes.
Entrances (fade, slide, pop, wipe) play when the design's scene goes live.

Your details (name, Twitch, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, website, schedule) fill in {twitch} and the like in any design, and are shared with the other NorthRay apps. Anything not set is left out tidily.
Save as PNG puts a design at full size in Pictures › NorthRay Capture.
Audio plugins: put a plugin's DLL in the plugins folder (Settings › Plugins › Open the folder), check its signature and SHA-256, switch it on, then add it from a source's Filters page.
Nothing runs until you switch it on. A plugin whose file changes or goes missing is switched off again, and so is one that was running if Capture closed unexpectedly.
For plugin makers: the C interface and an example tremolo plugin are in the source (apps/capture/sdk).
Borders now go round the outside of a source instead of covering its edge, so the whole picture still shows. Saved PNG overlays include the ring's thickness.

Camera Border maker: right-click a camera (or anything in a scene) › Border… Round its corners or make it a circle, add a ring of colour (plain or a gradient) and a glow or drop shadow, and see it change live in the preview as you adjust it.
Six presets to start from: Clean white, Neon glow, Soft shadow, Circle, Gold frame and Thin and square.
Save as PNG writes the border with a clear inside to Pictures › NorthRay Capture, to use as an overlay anywhere.

Each streaming destination chooses its sound: the Stream mix, or one of the six recording tracks (Settings › Streaming › Sound). Destinations still share the video encode. Not yet tested on a live stream on Windows; please report how it goes.
A second output (Settings › Audio) plays any one mix on another device as well, such as a line out to a streaming PC.
Quick routing in a source's Send to menu: Stream and recordings, Recordings only, Stream only, or Only me.
The routing check warns if the second output would feed desktop audio back into itself, or shares the monitor's device.

Audio filters: right-click a sound source in the Audio mixer › Filters. Gain, noise gate, noise suppression, expander, compressor, limiter, equaliser, balance and delay, in the order you choose, each with its own switch and values.
Presets to start from: a microphone (clean and even), a game or music (kept in check), or a safety limiter.
Filters change the source's own sound before its volume and routing; its test clip records the result.

Video and sound files as a source (+ in Sources): one file or several played in turn, looping or shuffled if you like, with Pause, Play, From the start and Next in its menu. Its sound has its own channel in the Audio mixer.
Stinger transitions: a video plays over the switch and the scene changes at the moment you choose (Transition › Stinger).
Custom shader transitions: write your own in HLSL (Transition › Custom shader › Make an example file to start from). If it doesn't compile, the menu says why and a fade is used.
Groups: right-click a source › Group with to move, resize and hide several sources as one; Ungroup puts them back.
Not yet: web pages as sources.
Scene folders: right-click a scene › Folder to put it in a folder. The Scenes list shows each folder as a heading with its scenes under it.

Export a scene to a file, and import one (right-click a scene). The file holds the scene, any scenes shown inside it, and their sources and placements; it never holds stream keys. Images and other files are referred to where they are, not copied in.
An imported scene gets names that don't clash with yours, and its placements are resized if it was made for a different canvas size.

New sources (+ in Sources): an image (animated GIFs play, and the picture updates by itself when the file is changed), text, a colour, a slideshow of a folder's images, and part of the screen (drag a rectangle over a still of your desktop).
Text has its own settings in its menu: the words, font, size, colour, bold, italic, alignment, line wrapping, and an outline with its colour.
Every source's menu now has Position and size (type the numbers), Rotation, Opacity and Duplicate.
Images, text, colours and slideshows can be partly see-through; what's behind them shows.

Transitions: switching scenes can now cut, fade, slide, swipe or luma wipe. Choose it under Transition in Controls, with its duration (0.15 to 2 seconds) and easing, the direction for slides and swipes, and the pattern and edge for luma wipes. Recordings and streams show the transition too.

Studio Mode (Controls): the preview splits into Preview, where you prepare a scene without anyone seeing, and Program, what's live (red frame). Transition, or Ctrl+Enter, puts the preview live. The Scenes list marks the live scene, and the preview warns you when you're editing the scene that's live.
Scenes inside scenes: + in Sources › Scene shows another scene inside this one, like any other source (move it, resize it, crop it). Capture won't let a scene end up inside itself.
Not yet: stinger and custom shader transitions, and image, text and slideshow sources (next).

Multistreaming: stream to several places at once (up to six), straight from Capture, with no restreaming service. Add destinations in Settings › Streaming, each with its own service, server, stream key and bitrate.
Destinations at the same bitrate share one encode, so the video is encoded once; a destination at a different bitrate (say Twitch at 6 Mbit/s and YouTube at 8) gets its own.

Each destination has its own connection, buffer and reconnection: one dropping or failing never stops the others. In Controls, each has its own row (live time, bitrate, dropped frames, reconnections, or why it stopped); click a row to start or stop just that one.
Settings › Streaming shows the upload all the switched-on destinations need, and lets you choose the longest wait between reconnection attempts.
Your 0.6 streaming settings and stream key carry over as the first destination.
Signing in to Twitch and YouTube has been taken out again: stream keys are pasted in, per destination.

Please note: the destinations were tested here with four local test servers at once (stopping one, adding one, one reconnecting by itself). This computer has no H.264 or AAC encoders, so the shared encode and streaming to real platforms haven't been tried yet.

Sign in to Twitch or YouTube (Settings › Streaming › Account) and Capture gets your stream key itself each time you go live, and for YouTube the server too, so a key reset on the website is picked up.
Twitch: your browser opens Twitch's page with a code to approve; Capture shows the same code so you can check. YouTube: you sign in with Google in your browser.

Capture asks only to read the stream key (Twitch) or to read your YouTube account (YouTube): it can't post, change your channel or read your messages. Sign-ins are kept in Windows Credential Manager; Sign out removes them and cancels them with Twitch or Google.

Please note: signing in needs NorthRay Capture to be registered with Twitch and Google, which hasn't happened yet, so in this version the Account row says it isn't set up and the stream key is entered as before. The sign-in itself has been tested here against a stand-in for both services, not the real ones.
Streaming: Start streaming in Controls. Choose Twitch, YouTube, Kick or a custom server in Settings › Streaming, and enter your stream key.
The stream key is kept in Windows Credential Manager on this PC. It's never shown, and never written to settings or logs. A key pasted on the end of a server address is moved there too.
Secure streaming (RTMPS) uses Windows' own TLS, and Capture checks the server's certificate itself: a wrong name or an untrusted authority is refused, with the reason.

If the connection drops, Capture keeps going and reconnects by itself (after 2 seconds, then longer, up to a minute). A stream key the platform refuses isn't retried. If the network can't keep up, old frames are dropped rather than the stream falling behind, and counted in the status bar.
The status bar shows the stream's state, time, bitrate and dropped frames. Recording and streaming can run together.

Please note: streaming has been tested here against a local test server, over plain and secure connections. This computer has no H.264 or AAC encoders, so it hasn't yet run with a real encoder or to a real platform. If it doesn't work, the message and the log (Settings › Open the logs folder) say why.
Not yet: streaming to several platforms at once (next) and saving a recording as MP4.

Recording: Start recording in Controls. The canvas is encoded as H.264 by your graphics card's encoder where it has one (NVIDIA, AMD or Intel), or by Windows' software encoder, with the recording tracks chosen in Settings › Recording as AAC audio tracks, each named after the sources on it.

Recordings are MKV files in Videos\NorthRay Capture (or the folder you choose). They're written so that everything up to a crash or power cut still plays. Recording stops cleanly if the disk is nearly full.
Settings › Recording: the folder, the video encoder (automatic or a chosen one), video quality (6 to 40 Mbit/s), which audio tracks go in the file, and audio quality.
While recording: the time in Controls, and the time, the file's size and any lost frames in the status bar.
A sync test source (+ in Sources › Sync test): a white flash and a beep at the start of each second, for checking that picture and sound line up in a recording.

Please note: recording has only been tested here as far as the file format. This computer has no H.264 or AAC encoders, so recording hasn't yet run with a real encoder. If it doesn't work on your PC, the message and the log (Settings › Open the logs folder) say why.
Not yet: streaming (next) and saving a recording as MP4.

Audio routing: each sound source can be sent to the stream (what viewers hear), recording tracks 1 to 6, and the monitor (what you hear) independently, with the buttons under its fader or “Send to” in its right-click menu. A source that isn't sent to the stream is absent from it, not just turned down.
New sources start on the stream and track 1 (everything), plus a track of their own kind: microphones on 2, desktop audio on 3, programs on 4, ready for editing later.
Monitoring: the monitor mix plays on the device chosen in Settings › Audio (Windows' default to begin with). The mixer shows meters for the stream and the monitor.

Warnings in the mixer when a program kept off the stream would still reach viewers through desktop audio, when the same sound reaches a mix twice, when monitoring desktop audio would feed back into itself, and when a microphone could pick up monitoring played through speakers. A leak can be fixed in one click (on Windows 11): desktop audio leaves that program out.
Desktop audio can leave one program out (right-click › Leave a program out, Windows 11). Windows allows one program per desktop audio source.
Settings › Audio lists where each sound source goes, and any problems.
Save a 10-second test clip of the stream mix, any track or the monitor (right-click a sound source › Save a test clip of a mix).
The mixer scrolls with the mouse wheel when its sources don't all fit.

Sound capture: add a microphone or other input, desktop audio (everything an output device plays) or, on Windows 11, one program's sound on its own from + in the Audio mixer (or in Sources). A program is found by name, so its sound is captured again whenever it restarts; sources set to Windows' default device follow it when it changes.

The Audio mixer: a level meter for each sound source and for the mix (green, yellow and red, with a line at the recent peak), a volume fader showing decibels, and a mute button. Sound sources are heard in every scene.

Right-click a sound source to rename it, change its device or program, mute it, remove it, or save a 10-second test clip of just its own sound (before its volume and mute) to Videos\NorthRay Capture, so you can hear exactly what it captures.
Click a sound source's name to see its whole status, such as why a device can't be used.
Not yet: separate stream, recording and headphone mixes (next), recording and streaming.
Video capture: add a whole display, a window or a camera or capture card from + in Sources, and see it live in the preview.

Displays are captured with Desktop Duplication, or Windows Graphics Capture or a slower compatibility mode where that isn't available; you can choose the method and whether to show the mouse pointer from a source's right-click menu.

Windows are captured with Windows Graphics Capture (they can be covered by other windows). Capture remembers the program and finds its window again when it restarts; minimised windows keep their last picture.

Arrange sources on the preview: drag to move, drag the handles to resize (Shift for any shape), Alt+drag a handle to crop, with snapping to the edges and centre of the canvas (hold Ctrl to place freely). The arrow keys nudge (Shift for 10 pixels).

Each source's right-click menu: rename, hide, lock, fit to the canvas (Ctrl+F), stretch (Ctrl+S), centre (Ctrl+D), reset (Ctrl+R), rotate, flip, remove the crop, and order. The eye and lock buttons in Sources hide and lock.
A source can be shown in several scenes (“A source from another scene” under +) and is captured once.
The status bar shows how long the graphics card takes for each frame, and the preview shows the frame rate being kept.
Not yet: sound, recording and streaming.
First version, in early development: the foundation. It doesn't capture, record or stream yet.

The workspace: a preview area and Scenes, Sources, Audio mixer and Controls panels. Drag the dividers to resize, drag a panel's header (or right-click it) to move or hide it, and save, load or reset layouts from Layout in the top bar.
Scenes: add, rename, duplicate, reorder and delete, switch with Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+9 or the arrow keys; saved automatically.
Settings: theme, low-resource mode, preview and output frame rates, canvas size, the encoders found on your PC, the logs folder and Copy diagnostics.
Coming next: capturing displays, windows and cameras, with a live preview and moving and resizing sources on it.
